summary: Help 7-8 year-olds represent sums and differences within 100 on a number line by mapping calculation onto MAGNITUDE: numbers are positions/lengths, a jump's LENGTH is the amount added or subtracted (not its endpoint), addition is a forward jump and subtraction a backward jump. The key representational demands are that intervals (not tick marks) carry the quantity, spacing is proportional, and jumps can be partitioned to mirror place-value strategy (38 + 27 as +20 then +7). The target tool is the empty number line, and children should both READ a given diagram and DRAW their own.
misconceptions: Counting tick marks (points) instead of intervals/jumps — off-by-one errors
Unequal or non-proportional spacing so distance doesn't represent magnitude
Reading a jump as its endpoint rather than as the amount added/subtracted
Drawing subtraction as a forward jump, or starting an addition jump from 0 rather than from the first number

activities.title: Build the jump: make each arrow's length equal the amount
steps: Start at 38 on a number line and add a forward jump of 20, then a forward jump of 7, landing on 58 then 65 (showing 38 + 27 = 65).
Notice and state that the +20 jump is drawn visibly longer than the +7 jump because the LENGTH of the jump is the amount.
Build 52 − 24 yourself using backward (leftward) jumps, e.g. −20 then −4, or −22 then −2 bridging 30, landing on 28.
Label each jump with its size and label the start and end points.
Both interpret a diagram you are given and construct one for a new calculation.
activities.insight: Distance on the line equals the amount: a jump represents 'add/subtract this much', not the point it lands on. Addition moves forward and subtraction moves backward, and partitioning a jump mirrors the mental place-value strategy.

activities.title: Label the spaces, not the marks
steps: On a pre-marked, equally spaced number line, label the SPACES (intervals) between the marks rather than the marks themselves.
Physically step out a jump, counting the gaps crossed, not the ticks touched.
Check an endpoint: for a jump of 20 from 38, confirm it lands on 58 and not one mark off.
activities.insight: The amount is the number of intervals jumped, not the number of tick marks counted — this is the classic off-by-one trap.

activities.title: Interpret a given diagram, then draw your own
steps: Interpret: shown a number line starting at 38 with an arrow landing on 58 labelled '+20' and then an arrow landing on 65 labelled '+7', state what calculation it shows (38 + 27 = 65) and what each jump means.
Explain that 27 has been partitioned into 20 and 7, each a forward jump of that amount.
Translate: on a blank line, draw a number line to show 52 − 24, using backward jumps totalling 24, landing on 28, with start, end, and each jump labelled and spaced proportionally.
Match number-line diagrams to the equations they represent.
activities.insight: Reading a diagram and faithfully producing one are different skills; full command means you can do both, reading jumps as amounts and drawing proportional, correctly-directed lines.

checkQuestion: First, interpretation: show the child a number line starting at 38 with two arrows drawn — a jump landing on 58 labelled '+20', then a jump landing on 65 labelled '+7'. Ask: 'What calculation does this picture show, and what does each jump mean?' Then, translation: hand them a blank line and say 'Now draw a number line to show 52 − 24.'
checkAnswer: Interpretation: it shows 38 + 27 = 65, with 27 partitioned into 20 and 7, each arrow a forward jump of that amount (a jump = an addition of its length). Translation: a number line from 52 with backward jump(s) totalling 24 (e.g. −20 then −4, or −22 then −2 bridging 30) landing on 28, start and end labelled, jumps sized and labelled, points spaced proportionally.
